title: Charting the Three Waves of Legal AI Transformation with Thomson Reuters' Raghu Ramanathan
author: Raghu Ramanathan

dom.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment

st.t: AI procurement: Product expansion exceeds realized value
st.an: The source shifts attention from buyer-side workflow fit, realised value and renewal economics to vendor-side commercial support and education. It suggests that better-informed vendors may improve market functioning, but presents this as a hope and does not substantively assess whether AI products generate realised organisational value.
qs: but there’s very little to support vendors and yet they have their own pain points, many of which are in common with one another.

st.t: Associate training: Automation threatens expertise reproduction
st.an: Ramanathan anticipates AI-driven redesign of pricing, pyramid staffing and lawyers’ work, but does not engage the cluster’s central concern that automating junior work may undermine expertise reproduction or require reconstructed apprenticeship. He instead prioritises shifting lawyers toward higher-value activities and teaching them to delegate to AI assistants.

st.t: Organisational adaptation: AI benefits require human control
st.an: The source contains only closing remarks, contact information and credits, with no substantive claims or evidence about whether legal AI’s benefits depend on organisational adaptation and human control. Its position relative to the cluster therefore cannot be determined.

st.t: Agentic workflows: Tacit expertise resists easy transfer

It also identifies document–research integration as an important workflow challenge, although that point is interviewer framing and the performance claims remain company-reported without disclosed validation.

And then we redeployed our editorial team, which you know about, which used to create all these editorials for Westlaw Practical Law, and said, can you create new, different content just to help us with the claims explorer?

st.an: Ramanathan accepts the need to assess AI across whole legal matters rather than isolated tasks and materially develops the cluster by proposing end-to-end outcome benchmarking. st.an: The source accepts that AI requires redesigned staffing, workflows and lawyer development, and materially extends the cluster by proposing equity incentives for technology talent and curricula focused on delegation, technology and unstructured problem solving. st.t: Production model: Institutional absorption governs AI value
st.an: Ramanathan accepts that AI value requires organisational and workforce redesign, then materially extends the cluster by identifying two specific absorption mechanisms: reforming law-firm equity to attract technology talent and teaching lawyers to delegate effectively to AI assistants. His claims are predictive and anecdotal rather than measured evidence of workforce outcomes.

st.t: Service model: AI challenges production more than lawyers
st.an: Ramanathan accepts the cluster’s core view that near-term AI augments rather than replaces lawyers and primarily transforms workflows, pricing and staffing. He materially extends it with a staged three-wave transformation model and a concrete recommendation to measure AI’s end-to-end effect across matters rather than isolated model output.

st.t: Service redesign: Resistance reflects incentives and identity
st.an: Ramanathan aligns with the cluster’s emphasis on concrete customer workflows and deliberate, feedback-led experimentation. He adds a practical prioritisation method that combines potential workflow value, near-term technical feasibility and rapid customer validation, while not addressing the cluster’s broader claims about incentives, leadership or organisational identity.
qs: If we could do this, how much of a breakthrough difference is it to the workflows of our customers?
And the second thing is technical feasibility, because otherwise the product team will go with some amazing ideas, but perhaps very, very low chance of realizing in the next six months.

st.t: Vendor market: Expanding maps require disciplined selection
st.an: Shaver accepts the need for disciplined market navigation and materially extends it to the vendor side, identifying shared procurement and business-development information gaps and presenting tailored intermediary support as the response. For example, they all deal with security questionnaires, they deal with a long sales cycle of law firms, and they also have areas where a lot of legal tech startup founders and CEOs need information, but there’s not a lot available.

kp.k: Three waves progress from optimisation to business-model transformation
kp.d: Ramanathan presents a predictive framework: the current optimisation wave improves existing work's speed and quality; a re-engineering wave expected shortly changes activity allocation, pricing and staffing; a third wave changes firms' roles in the legal ecosystem. Asked whether the third wave would arrive by 2028, he considers that slightly early and forecasts 2030–2035.
qs: the first wave, which we are in the middle of right now, is what we call the optimization wave.
How do I re-engineer my pricing?  How do I re-engineer my staffing models, my pyramid model, all of that, right?
So let’s say 2030 to 2035, I think that will happen.

kp.k: Reported adoption and benefits use different measures
kp.d: Ramanathan reports surveys in which 24 % of firms considered themselves AI pioneers and had adopted AI, with 94 % of that subset reporting concrete benefits. Separately, he says internal data show 20 to 23 % of firms now have AI access, compared with his estimate of one, two, three percent adoption when he joined approximately 12 months earlier. The transcript supplies no sample sizes or survey methods, and access, adoption and self-described leadership are distinct reported measures.
qs: we found that 24 % of law firms already considered themselves leaders in pioneering AI and had already adopted AI. And 94 % of this 24 % were already getting concrete benefits
the adoption of AI in the legal industry was in the very low single digit, probably one, two, three percent.
what we are finding with our own data is now 20 to 23 % of law firms have access to AI.

kp.k: Earlier automation predictions included an acknowledged failed forecast
kp.d: Reflecting on his 2017 professional-services paper, Ramanathan recounts predictions that bots would perform 66 % of legal associates' work, 90 to 95 % of accountants would disappear, pricing would become outcome-based, and firms would deliver technology through apps. He explicitly identifies the prediction that the largest firms would have no lawyers and instead use freelance networks as having failed; the other historical predictions are not established findings in this interview.
qs: 66 % of legal associates work would be done by bots
like 90 to 95 % of the accountants would be gone.
professional services companies or law firms would not have any lawyers. It would be a freelance network that they’re working in, right? Which of course didn’t come true.

kp.k: Future firms may sell technology and outcome-based services
kp.d: Ramanathan predicts commoditised technology-based services, entry into related business areas beyond traditional law, and movement beyond fixed fees toward true outcome-based pricing. He reports conversations with progressive firms exploring changes to the legal value chain, including potentially self-cannibalising direct-to-consumer models. These are anticipated or exploratory developments, not evidence of market-wide implementation.
qs: There will be a commoditized tech-based service that is offered.
They will get into new lines of business, which go beyond where you traditionally think law stops
There will be more, even more advances on pricing and, you know, to true outcome base as opposed to just fix fee models.
perhaps even cannibalizing themselves in some cases, direct to consumer models.

kp.k: Leaner staffing need not mean lower total headcount
kp.d: Explicitly noting disagreement among the report's authors, Ramanathan offers his personal view that the pyramid will become leaner and hiring competition will shift toward partners rather than associates. He does not expect necessarily fewer people or lawyers because efficiency could unlock demand. His supporting analogy is cloud consulting: projects formerly taking three years could take six months, prompting customers to commission more projects; he describes Accenture's business as subsequently two, three, four X bigger.
qs: we had some disagreement between the authors of the report.
I do think it’s gonna become more of a leaner model and the pressure will be on hiring more partners
But I don’t necessarily believe that the number of people in the law firm are gonna go down.
Because lots of customers said, hey, if I can do such innovations in six months instead of three years, I have more projects for you.

kp.k: Improved economics could unlock corporate demand for firms
kp.d: Responding to the host's question about work moving in-house, Ramanathan reports that legal departments he speaks with face tightening budgets, need greater efficiency, and have more issues than time even when bringing work inside. He says they report broader executive-level responsibilities and delaying law-firm engagement because of the price-value equation. He predicts AI-driven changes to that equation will bring additional demand to firms.
qs: Most of them I’m talking to are saying that the first challenge is that the budget is tightening.
they’re saying, look, we’d love to engage with law firms, but because of the price value equation, we had to start later with them
I do believe that with AI, with the adjustment of the price value equation, more of that demand will come to the law firms as well.

kp.k: Technology recruitment may require different equity structures
kp.d: Ramanathan expects firms to need more technology talent alongside partners, while acknowledging difficulty mixing their cultures. He argues that firms must offer equity opportunities competitive with technology employers' stock options, and reports managing partners exploring alternative holding structures. He explicitly does not explain how these changes would be implemented.
qs: So more partners, more tech talent
I don’t know how, so don’t ask me how, but I do think that the equity structure of law firms need to change in order for tech talent to thrive.
they’ve been looking at alternative holding structures, how to actually give more equity to tech talent.

kp.k: AI assistance changes lawyer skills and educational needs
kp.d: Ramanathan frames AI as an assistant rather than a replacement and argues that lawyers must learn delegation instead of doing everything themselves. He identifies technology skills and broader unstructured problem-solving as additional competencies and recommends different curricula. His account contrasts these needs with lawyers' existing analytical thoroughness and attention to detail.
qs: AI is like an assistant, it’s by your side, you gotta learn delegation
If you try to do it all yourself, you’re not gonna be successful in this new world.
technology, delegation, more broader unstructured problem solving are new skills that a lawyer needs to pick up. And that’s why I think the curriculums need to be different too.

kp.k: Complex AI capabilities require editorial expertise and experimentation
kp.d: Ramanathan describes CoCounsel as having about 20 skills and moving toward harder, riskier capabilities under competitive pressure. Claims Explorer initially produced unhelpful results when identifying potential claims from facts and jurisdiction; repurposing the Westlaw and Practical Law editorial team to create targeted content improved it. He claims it now identifies two times more valid claims than a lawyer can manually identify in the available time, without providing testing methods or sample details.
qs: As of last count, I think we have about 20 skills
the answer that we’re getting back from our AI from co-counsel was actually not that very useful
can you create new, different content just to help us with the claims explorer?
it comes up with two times more valid claims than a lawyer can manually do in the time that they have.

kp.k: Integrated content and longer context improve legal workflows
kp.d: Ramanathan says CoCounsel's approach has shifted from relying on Thomson Reuters content toward combining it with customer documents and public data. He attributes improved performance and speed partly to advances in underlying models, specifically Google's longer context window, which reduces the need to subdivide uploaded material. These are vendor-reported technical benefits rather than quantified comparative findings.
qs: Today, all these scales run off TR data, the customer data, public data, all meshing together.
we work with all of the leading LLMs, and each has the strengths and weaknesses.
they came up with a long context window, which means you can upload a lot of the data without having to parse, without having to subdivide.

kp.k: Workflow value and feasibility guide product investment
kp.d: Ramanathan says Thomson Reuters prioritises new capabilities using two criteria: the magnitude of improvement to customer workflows and technical feasibility, including the chance of delivering within the next six months. A core customer innovation community provides early feedback on whether proposed capabilities would be useful if they worked.
qs: If we could do this, how much of a breakthrough difference is it to the workflows of our customers?
And the second thing is technical feasibility
perhaps very, very low chance of realizing in the next six months.
Would you be interested if this works? If this works, right? And then they give us immediate feedback.

kp.k: Court AI adoption targets backlogs and access pressures
kp.d: Ramanathan links AI's judicial importance to constrained budgets, access-to-justice concerns and his reported 40 % increase in pending federal district-court cases over four years compared with 2020. He reports an agreement for federal courts to deploy Thomson Reuters AI across 25,000 judges and staff, and says 45 out of 50 states use its CoCounsel and Westlaw AI. These adoption statements do not establish measured backlog reductions or access improvements.
qs: Compared to 2020, in four years, we have 40 % more pending cases in the district Courts in the federal codes
there is a real issue of access to justice, and the budgets are not going to get any easier
the federal courts are going to deploy  Thomson Reuters AI across 25,000 users, judges, and court staff
45 out of 50 states now are using AI that we have provided with co-council and Westlaw AI.

kp.k: Judicial education partnership extends into policy development
kp.d: Ramanathan describes the Thomson Reuters Institute–National Center of State Courts partnership as educating judges and court staff and increasingly helping participants understand and shape policy developments. He reports over 10,000 judges and court staff joining its monthly webinars during the preceding six months, alongside requests for demonstrations and sandbox experimentation.
qs: this association is now getting into the heart of helping understand policy developments. how to shape policy developments as well
in the last six months, Marlene, we’ve had over 10,000 judges and court staff join this
To test running, working in a sandbox, getting their hands dirty.

kp.k: Individual adoption requires substantial hands-on support
kp.d: Ramanathan argues that AI's many possible uses can overwhelm users, making product sales insufficient to deliver value. He reports growing customer-success staffing from less than 10 at the beginning of the previous year to over 200 specialists. Their work focuses on individual lawyers, from login setup to applying AI to current matters. A practice-specific use-case library draws on legally and technically knowledgeable staff and customer experiences, excluding customer-designated proprietary examples.
qs: if the customer, the end user, the lawyer is not using it or the judge is not using it, it counts for nothing
less than 10 people beginning of last year, to now over 200 customer success specialists
they know enough about law and they know enough about technology
If a customer says, hey, this is a use case that’s proprietary, I don’t want you to share, we don’t share it.

kp.k: Benchmarks should measure end-to-end assisted legal outcomes
kp.d: Ramanathan supports industry benchmarks and reports participation in the recent Vals AI study, but criticises some benchmarks as insufficiently relevant to practice. Because he expects lawyers to remain involved for at least the next couple of years, he recommends measuring AI's effect across an entire matter or outcome rather than only isolated outputs. The interview provides no Vals AI results or specific internal benchmark metrics.
qs: We participated in the recent VALS AI study
we are not in a phase where AI is replacing the lawyers, at least not in the next couple of years.
the AI output is one step of a multi-step legal workflow.
Why don’t we benchmark the end-to-end impact of that AI output across the entire matter or entire outcome

kp.k: Smaller firms' adoption may intensify competitive pressure
kp.d: Ramanathan reports observing faster AI movement among small and medium firms, which see it as a competitive equaliser. He predicts larger firms will need faster change and bolder moves to avoid rapidly emerging imitations of their offerings. He supplies no comparative adoption data for firm-size groups.
qs: small and medium law firms are moving faster with AI
they are seeing this as a competitive tool, weapon, an equalizer
large law firms will have to up the game and change things quite fast
I think you’re going to see more bolder moves by the larger law firms

kp.k: Change management becomes a central competitive differentiator
kp.d: Ramanathan argues that successful transformation increasingly depends less on technology alone and more on strategic clarity, organisational alignment and operational change management. He predicts that firms enabling rank-and-file staff to embrace and benefit from AI will distinguish themselves from laggards.
qs: it is becoming less and less about technology. It is more about change management.
operational change management to make sure that the rank and file of the organizations actually benefit, embrace
that’s gonna differentiate winners from people who are lagging.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: Ramanathan predicts three waves of legal AI transformation: optimization of existing work, re-engineering of firms, and new business models, alongside changes in staffing, demand, competition and judicial operations.
pts.d: Raghu Ramanathan, Thomson Reuters' president of legal professionals, predicts that legal and healthcare will lead AI transformation, with legal ahead because healthcare faces greater regulatory and privacy challenges. His three-wave account starts with faster, better existing legal work; proceeds to redesigning lawyer activities, pricing and staffing; and culminates in commoditized technology-based services, adjacent business lines, genuinely outcome-based pricing rather than merely fixed fees, and potentially self-cannibalizing direct-to-consumer offerings. His personal staffing prediction, which he says was disputed among the report's authors, is a leaner pyramid, competition shifting toward partners rather than associates, and more technology talent, but not necessarily lower total firm headcount. He expects cheaper and faster delivery to unlock additional demand, including work from corporate legal departments despite their bringing some work in-house. He predicts changes to firm equity structures to attract technology talent and greater emphasis on lawyers' technology skills, delegation and unstructured problem-solving, with corresponding curriculum changes. On products, he says CoCounsel's Claims Explorer produces twice as many valid claims as a lawyer can manually identify in the available time, following development of supporting editorial content; combining Thomson Reuters, customer and public content, and advances in LLM context windows, improve output and speed. He presents court AI as a response to rising pending caseloads, constrained budgets and access-to-justice problems. He observes smaller and medium-sized firms moving faster on AI, creating competitive pressure for larger firms to make bolder moves. He predicts strategic clarity and operational change management, rather than technology alone, will distinguish successful adopters. Separately, he recounts his 2017 predictions that bots would perform 66% of legal associates' work, professional services would move to outcome pricing and technology offerings, and the largest firms would operate through freelance networks without employed lawyers; he explicitly identifies the last prediction as failed.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The evidence offered combines reported Thomson Reuters survey and adoption data, product-development experience, customer conversations, court agreements and a software-industry analogy; the broader structural changes remain forecasts.
pts.d: Ramanathan reports surveys in which 24% of firms considered themselves AI pioneers and had adopted AI, with 94% of that subgroup reporting concrete benefits. Separately, he cites company data indicating that 20–23% of firms have access to AI, compared with his estimate of 1–3% adoption when he joined approximately a year earlier. The transcript does not provide survey samples, field dates, definitions or methods; access, adoption and reported benefits should remain distinct measures. His expectation of expanding legal demand draws on his software-industry experience: cloud implementation shortened projects, but clients commissioned more projects and consulting businesses grew. Conversations with corporate legal departments supply the rationale that budget constraints and an unfavorable price–value relationship suppress engagement with firms. Conversations with managing partners support his account of interest in alternative equity structures and new business models. The Claims Explorer claim is a vendor-reported performance comparison and development account, without an accompanying test protocol, sample or independent validation in the transcript. He reports that combining content sources and longer LLM context windows improved product performance. For courts, he cites a 40% rise in pending federal district court cases over four years from 2020, without identifying the underlying dataset; an agreement for AI deployment to 25,000 federal judicial users; use of Thomson Reuters AI on the state-court side in 45 states; and over 10,000 judges and court staff joining partnership webinars over six months. These are offered as evidence of need, uptake and enthusiasm, not measured reductions in backlogs or improved access to justice. He mentions participation in the Vals AI study but supplies no results, and advocates benchmarking entire legal workflows rather than standalone AI output. The three-wave model, relative pace of legal versus healthcare transformation, competitive redistribution and change-management predictions rest on his interpretation and experience rather than a quantified forecast presented here.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: Optimization is current in the 2025 interview, re-engineering is imminent, and the new-business-model wave is forecast for approximately 2030–2035; near-term AI is framed as lawyer augmentation.
pts.d: Ramanathan places firms in the first wave at the time of the interview and says the second will start shortly. He considers 2028 slightly early for the third wave and instead specifies five to ten years, approximately 2030–2035. He explicitly says AI is not replacing lawyers in the next couple of years and treats its output as one step in a multi-step legal workflow. His staffing forecast is qualified as his personal view, not an agreed position among all report authors; he does not guarantee stable employment, but rejects an inevitable decline in lawyer numbers. Demand expansion is conditional on AI improving the price–value equation and freeing capacity for additional problems. Attracting technology talent is tied to changing equity arrangements, but he expressly declines to specify how those changes will work. Successful adoption is conditional on actual end-user use, strategic alignment and operational change management; product sales and technical capability alone are insufficient. Product ambitions are qualified by rapidly changing models, technical feasibility, experimentation and acknowledged misses. Competition and change-management predictions are made in response to a question about the next couple of years, without more precise deadlines. Historical automation predictions date to his 2017 paper and should not be read as newly validated estimates or assigned the 2030–2035 timetable.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The predicted changes affect firms' staffing and competitive positions, lawyers' skills, corporate buyers' purchasing decisions, technology talent, judicial personnel and people seeking justice.
pts.d: For law firms, Ramanathan anticipates redesigned staffing pyramids, pricing, service portfolios and possibly ownership structures. Partners become a stronger hiring priority relative to associates; he does not translate the historical prediction about associates' tasks into a current numerical job-loss forecast. Technology professionals become more important and require competitive equity incentives. Practicing lawyers need to delegate to AI assistants and concentrate on higher-value, less structured work; legal education needs to adapt. Small and medium firms may use AI as a competitive equalizer, while large firms face pressure to differentiate and innovate more boldly. Corporate legal departments are buyers under budget pressure, with expanding executive-level responsibilities and more issues than available time; better-priced external services could make earlier or greater engagement with law firms attractive even alongside insourcing. Courts, judges and court staff are presented as enthusiastic adopters who can use AI to address workload pressures; the wider public is implicated through the stated access-to-justice problem, although the interview supplies no measured public outcomes. Thomson Reuters and other vendors face pressure to develop more ambitious capabilities and support actual use: Ramanathan reports expanding customer-success staffing from fewer than 10 at the beginning of the previous year to over 200, emphasizing assistance for individual lawyers rather than management alone.
